pages.text: Sulfuric acid is made in greater tonnage than any other chemical, some 270 million tonnes a year. The Factory Must Grow's way, three sulfur dust and a nitrate dust with 1,000 mB of water in a vat for 500 mB, is the lead chamber process in small, nitre carrying oxygen to the burning sulfur as in Roebuck's chambers of 1746.
pages.title: Sulfuric acid

pages.text: It is hard on sulfur and on nitre. Phillips patented the contact process in 1831, and from about 1900, when Knietsch made it work at BASF, it took over.

First, sulfur dioxide. A sulfur dust burnt in 1,000 mB of air in a heated basin gives 500 mB. Or catch it off the roasters: two raw sphalerite, chalcopyrite, pentlandite or galena with 500 mB of air in a heated basin roast to their oxide or calcine and give 250 mB of it, and two molybdenite with 1,000 mB give 500.
pages.title: Sulfur dioxide

pages.text: Every modern copper, zinc and nickel smelter runs an acid plant on its roaster gas, which pays for the plant and keeps the gas out of the valleys downwind. Roasted on a campfire, it goes into the air. It is a heavy, choking gas; pipe it away before it boils out of the basin.

Sulfur dioxide will not take a second oxygen by itself. Over vanadium pentoxide at about 430 °C it does, and the cooler the bed the further it goes, so a converter is three or four catalyst beds with coolers between.
pages.title: The converter

pages.text: A heated vat with no machine in it is the bed: a vanadium pentoxide, 500 mB of sulfur dioxide and 500 mB of air give 500 mB of sulfur trioxide, and the catalyst back 49 times in 50. Platinum was the first catalyst; vanadium, cheaper and not poisoned by arsenic, replaced it from the 1920s.

The trioxide is never put into water, which turns it to a fog of acid no scrubber catches. Strong acid absorbs it: 500 mB of trioxide stirred into 500 mB of sulfuric acid give 500 mB of oleum, fuming sulfuric acid, and oleum let down with 500 mB of water gives 1,000 mB of sulfuric acid.
pages.title: Absorption

pages.text: That is 500 mB more for every sulfur dust, three times the lead chamber's, and no nitre. The trioxide and oleum fume and are poison to breathe.

Vanadium rides in magnetite, a fraction of a per cent of it, and most of the world's comes out of titanomagnetite. Four raw magnetite with a soda ash and 500 mB of water, superheated, are the salt roast and the water leach: 250 mB of sodium vanadate liquor, and three crushed iron ore still good to smelt.
pages.title: Vanadium pentoxide

pages.text: 250 mB of the liquor and an ammonium chloride, heated, throw down ammonium metavanadate, which calcines to a vanadium pentoxide, orange-brown.
Most of the world's sulfur is not mined. Crude oil and gas carry it, up to a few per cent, and a refinery must take it out or the fuel burns to sulfur dioxide.
pages.title: Sulfur from oil

pages.text: The hydrotreater is a heated vat with no machine in it, over a cobalt-molybdenum bed: a cobalt sulfate, a molybdenum oxide and four bauxite powder, heated, make four, and the bed lasts 19 runs in 20.

500 mB of heavy oil and 250 mB of hydrogen, the reformer's own, give 500 mB of diesel and 250 mB of hydrogen sulfide, the sulfur gone to the gas. The Claus unit burns a third of that and lets the rest react with it: 1,000 mB of hydrogen sulfide and 500 mB of air, heated, drop two sulfur dust.
Texas, Louisiana and the Persian Gulf make their sulfur this way and ship it to acid plants that have no sulfur of their own.
Before the oil, pyrite.
pages.title: Pyrite

pages.text: A pyrite lode is a lens of iron sulfide with a little chalcopyrite, sphalerite and galena through it, a massive sulfide, as at Rio Tinto, and for a century the acid works of Europe roasted it: two raw pyrite with 1,000 mB of air in a heated basin give 500 mB of sulfur dioxide and two raw hematite, the cinder, which the blast furnace still takes.
Huelva, downstream of Rio Tinto, is a copper-smelting acid hub to this day.

The Nether has the one ore with a reason to be there. Native sulfur is the yellow crust a fumarole leaves, on the basalt deltas and in the soul sand valleys, as the vents of Kawah Ijen leave it, where it is still carried down the crater by the basketful.
pages.title: Native sulfur

pages.text: A millstone or crushing wheels grind the raw crust to sulfur dust, and three sulfur dust with a nitrate in The Factory Must Grow's vat are its own acid.

Acid comes back, too. A refinery's alkylation unit makes high-octane gasoline over sulfuric acid: 500 mB of LPG with 100 mB of acid, cold, give 500 mB of gasoline and 100 mB of spent acid, black with oil and down to about 90%.
pages.title: Spent acid

pages.text: A regeneration plant cracks it in a furnace: 500 mB of spent acid and 250 mB of air, superheated, are 500 mB of sulfur dioxide, back to the converter.

Acid is made where the sulfur is burnt, not where the ore is dug. Nexa's Cajamarquilla refinery outside Lima made 345,000 tonnes of zinc in 2025 and 594,000 tonnes of acid with it, and sold nearly all the acid, by rail car and chemical tanker, to the copper leach plants of northern Chile at Mejillones and Barquito.
pages.title: Where it is made

pages.text: Kokkola in Finland made 290,000 tonnes of zinc and 312,000 of acid; Atlantic Copper's smelter at Huelva makes 1.1 million tonnes a year; Kamoa-Kakula's new smelter sells 40,000 tonnes a month to the Copperbelt's leach pads.
Only about 7% of the world's acid crosses a border: it is cheap, heavy and eats its tank, so a smelter's acid wants a fertiliser plant or a leach pad nearby, or a port.
